Slovak Steel Industry Reports Steady Output and Modest Growth in Latest Results

Bratislava – Slovakia’s steel industry continued its trajectory of stable performance in the first quarter of 2024, with major producers posting modest increases in both output and revenue, according to industry data released Tuesday. The results reflect ongoing resilience despite subdued demand in some export markets and fluctuating raw material costs.

The Slovak Steel Association, which represents the country’s principal steelmakers, reported a collective crude steel production of 1.28 million tonnes for the first three months of the year, marking a 2.1% increase over the same period last year. Revenue across the sector rose by 2.5% to €1.04 billion, buoyed by moderately higher steel prices and steady domestic demand from the construction and machinery sectors.

“Despite a challenging environment in parts of Europe, Slovak steel producers have managed to sustain growth,” said Radoslav Jurík, spokesperson for the association. “The sector’s stability can be attributed to efficient operations and ongoing investments in modernising production lines.”

Among the leading companies, Danube Steelworks posted a 2.8% gain in output, driven by orders for sheet and long products, primarily from regional infrastructure projects. “New bridge and road contracts are helping to support demand,” said Danube Steelworks CEO Lucia Kováčová. “Our focus on high-strength steels for the Slovak and Czech construction markets has delivered consistent results.”

Eastern Slovakia’s Metalform Holding also reported steady figures, with production volume up 1.9% and net profits rising to €37.5 million. The company highlighted energy efficiency upgrades completed last year as a factor in improved margins. “Investments in more efficient furnaces and recycling systems are paying off,” said Metalform Holding’s plant director, Ľuboš Horváth.

Export demand remained stable, with approximately 48% of Slovak steel output shipped abroad, mainly to neighbouring EU countries and the Balkans. While demand from the automotive sector was described as “mixed,” orders from machinery and construction clients helped offset any softness.

Union leaders welcomed the results, noting there have been no significant layoffs or workforce reductions. “Employment levels have been maintained, and the sector continues to provide quality jobs in our industrial regions,” said Milan Sýkora, chairman of the Slovak Metalworkers Union.

Analysts point to ongoing investments in green technologies as a positive sign for the industry’s long-term prospects. “Slovak mills are making incremental progress in reducing emissions and boosting recycling rates,” said Jana Hrušková, an industry analyst with Central Europe Market Insights.

The Slovak Steel Association forecasts continued stability in the remainder of 2024, with expectations for moderate growth as infrastructure investment and industrial activity remain supportive.
